title: ‘Summer House’ Enters A “New Chapter” After Landing Its First Emmy Recognition – Contenders TV Nominees Studio
full_text: Lindsay Hubbard , one of the stars of Bravo ’s Summer House , was doing an on-camera interview for a different reality show when shocking news broke that two of her Summer House castmates had gotten together. At the end of March, Amanda Batula, who was still married to Kyle Cooke, and West Wilson, who had previously dated Batula’s close friend Ciara Miller, released a statement about their budding relationship. Related Stories News ‘Summer House’ Season 10 Reunion Show Breaks Bravo Ratings Record Ahead Of Final Installment News Emmy Nominations 2026: The Complete List Carl Radke , fellow Summer House star, told Deadline that he saw the pair’s statement when he landed in Los Angeles and realized that Hubbard was in the middle of shooting confessionals for Summer House spinoff In the City . This required a quick pivot from producers, as they revealed during a conversation featuring Hubbard, fellow castmate Carl Radke, executive producer Jamie Jakimo and showrunner Trish Gold for Deadline’s Contenders Television: The Nominees Studio. Watch the conversation below and scroll down for more photos from the event. Jakimo, executive producer and SVP Programming at Summer House producer Truly Original, said, “When some news was put on the internet, we happened to have Lindsay in the studio with us. This is real. We follow what’s real, so we knew we had to camera up. We were on a green screen for a different show. This is happening now. Get the cameras. When something is newsworthy, noteworthy and affecting these cast members, we’re going to capture it.” The only problem was that the show was already in post and the reunion was coming up. “As producers, we’re learning things in real time, much like cast members,” Jakimo added. “We’ve become very nimble over the years where when we see things happening, when we get a call from somebody like Lindsay.” The scandal dominated the internet and continues to do so, and helped Summer House land its first-ever Emmy nomination after 10 seasons. The show is competing against the likes of Love on the Spectrum , America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders , RuPaul’s Drag Race: Untucked and Welcome to Wrexham in the Outstanding Unstructured Reality Program category. Hubbard told Deadline that she was “overwhelmed with excitement” about the nomination and joked that it was “overdue.” “Being recognized after 10 seasons is incredible,” Radke added. “We really are real friends, which of course provides a lot of ups and downs.” While the scandal involving Batula, Wilson and Miller may have got the headlines for Season 10, there were other storylines, including Hubbard and Radke becoming friends again after previously being together. “I was just excited and glad that [Lindsay] and I could continue to kind of grow the friendship, get some closure from the past, kind of try to move on with respect and try to build a new chapter of a friendship. You saw pieces of that like the conversation her and I had at the Labor Day party,” Radke said. “Watching it back was really meaningful and touching. She’s been just cool with me.” “We’re cooler than ever,” added Hubbard. 01 Carl Radke and Lindsay Hubbard Anthony Avellano for Deadline Lindsay Hubbard Anthony Avellano for Deadline L-R: Carl Radke; Jamie Jakimo and Trish Gold Anthony Avellano for Deadline L-R: Lindsay Hubbard, Jamie Jakimo, Trish Gold and Carl Radke Anthony Avellano for Deadline “We really tell these people’s stories,” added Gold. “It’s less about trying to make sure we get every little bit, but really rounding out everybody’s stories and being able to tell a complete story. How do we help move through this when relationships are fractured? One of the things that’s so pivotal is when Summer House is repairing relationships, because they are friends, and I think that’s unique to our show versus some of the other shows that are out there.” The cast is currently filming Season 11 in a new house as well as a crossover with Below Deck Mediterranean . Wilson and Batula are no longer on the show, but Hubbard, Radke, Cooke, Miller, Jesse Solomon, Bailey Taylor, KJ Dillard and Mia Calabrese are. “It feels good to be back. We’re like the little show that could. I feel like we have finally hit our stride. But now, it’s a new chapter,” said Radke. “It’s normal and natural for it to evolve with maybe some new faces or some people graduate or do whatever. It’s a totally new summer, but we have a new house.” Hubbard said that the whole situation “took a lot out of us.” She said, “We spent a lot of time on it, emotionally, mentally, physically. We were all ready to put it behind us and just celebrate a fresh start and a new house with a fun summer.” They’re all single now, as well, Hubbard stressed. “That makes for a fun summer.” Read More About: Comments

title: Scott Foley Returning To ‘Scrubs’ As Sean Kelly In Season 2 Of ABC Revival To Revisit Classic Storyline
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Scott Foley Returning To ‘Scrubs’ As Sean Kelly In Season 2 Of ABC Revival To Revisit Classic Storyline ‘Scrubs’ Adds Keyla Monterroso Mejia As New Nurse In Season 2 Of ABC Revival ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Renewed For Season 2 By HBO Max View All August 15, 2026 2:30pm Scott Foley/'Scrubs' Lebo Lukewarm/Paul Drinkwater/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images EXCLUSIVE : Cue the “Nobody cares, Sean” memes — Scott Foley is coming back to Scrubs . He will reprise his fan-favorite character Sean Kelly on the upcoming second season of the ABC revival. Related Stories Casting ‘Scrubs’ Adds Keyla Monterroso Mejia As New Nurse In Season 2 Of ABC Revival Casting ‘SNL’ Alum John Higgins Joins ‘Scrubs’ For Major Role In Season 2 Of ABC Revival Foley’s return is being announced today at D23’s “Scrubs : Scrubbing Back” panel moderated by Foley and featuring series stars/executive producers Zach Braff (John “J.D.” Dorian), Donald Faison (Christopher Turk) and Sarah Chalke (Elliot Reid), along with showrunner/executive producer Aseem Batra, which also teased more fantasy sequences and the comeback of J.D. beloved blue scooter Sasha next season. Deadline can reveal that Foley will be recurring and, in a full-circle moment, Sean will go back to where his journey on the show started, dating Elliot (Chalke). A Season 2 teaser, which you can watch below, provides a glimpse of Sean and Elliot’s reunion in the hospital cafeteria. Watch on Deadline The duo will be rekindling their romance just as Elliot’s ex-husband J.D. is embarking on a relationship with Charlie (Rachel Bilson), who was introduced in the Season 1 finale . “Scott Foley’s back to be love interest for Sarah, and Rachel has been mine; the dynamic with us all together is just hilarious, and we’re having so much fun,” Braff told Deadline. Added Chalke, “The writers were like, how do we bring back Elliot’s neurosis, and they thought that Scott would be a good way to do that.” She touched on that at D23, with Braff jumping in to announce Foley’s return. Chalke discussed Elliot and Sean’s reunion scene, in which she “falls gracefully” as her heel gets caught on her medical coat. Sarah Chalke is talking about Elliot’s neurosis and a moment she has in Season 2 when Zach Braff chimes in to reveal Scott Foley’s return as Sean Kelly More details here: https://t.co/KYVNyCE5L5 pic.twitter.com/H7d4fjCuyT — Deadline (@DEADLINE) August 15, 2026 Foley made his Scrubs debut at the end of Season 1, when Sean, a marine biologist and animal trainer at SeaWorld, was admitted to Sacred Heart with Elliot as his doctor. The two had a brief fling before she dumped him. Sean and Elliot reconnected again in Season 3 and dated for awhile, taking their relationship long-distance when Sean went to New Zealand. Elliot broke things off shortly after Sean returned as her romance with J.D. started to heat up, news Sean did not take well. He eventually moved on with J.D.’s baby mama Kim Briggs (Elizabeth Banks). Foley had been on Scrubs creator Bill Lawrence’s wish list for the revival for awhile. “I really want to have Scott Foley back, I want to have him back on the show just so Zach can say ‘Nobody cares, Sean,'” Lawrence said at PaleyFest in April, referring to the famous dismissive line J.D. uses in conversations with Sean on the original show. The catchphrase took on a life of its own and, two decades later, it continues to haunt Foley, with fans using it to respond to any post he puts up on social media. Foley brought up the infamous line when he came out on stage at D23. “This is personal for me. For those of your who don’t know, I played a character names Sean Kelly. Nobody cares, I heard that,” he said, adding, that he was part of “one of the most complicated love triangles in this show’s history.” Scott Foley takes the stage for the ‘Scrubs’ panel at #D23 to intro Zach Braff, Donald Faison and Sarah Chalke pic.twitter.com/Ha4fi2u6gH — Deadline (@DEADLINE) August 15, 2026 In a January interview, Foley revealed that Braff had asked him to return in Season 1 of the new Scrubs and that he had been scheduled for an episode but the schedule could not be worked out. “I’m sure we’ll find the time,” Foley said at the time as he was promoting his Prime Video series It’s Not Like That . The streamer ended up canceling the well received family drama after one season, and Foley’s two-season arc on Will Trent came to an end in May, rendering the Felicity and Scandal alum available . In Season 2 of Scrubs, J.D., Turk and Elliot have leveled up from interns to icons at Sacred Heart. Now, the respected doctors inspire the next generation while balancing the ups and downs of working in a hospital. Together with characters new and old, they are navigating this next chapter with laughter, heart and some surprises along the way. Foley’s return certainly qualifies as one of the surprises. Here is the trailer, which also teases the returns of other OGs from Season 1: In addition to Braff, Faison and Chalke, the Season 2 series regular cast includes Ava Bunn as intern Sam Tosh. The original series’ creator Bill Lawrence serves as executive producer on the revival via his Doozer Productions alongside the company’s Jeff Ingold and Liza Katzer as well as showrunner Batra and stars Braff, Faison and Chalke. Scrubs i s produced by 20th Television, a part of Disney Television Studios. The series will return to ABC Sept. 30 with a two-episode premiere, airing Wednesday and streaming next day on Hulu. In addition to Scrubs , Foley has done three other Bill Lawrence series, Cougar Town, Undateable and Whiskey Cavalier . His upcoming movies include Keep Coming Back and August . He is repped by Gersh and Atlas Artists. Natalie Sitek contributed to this report. It goes viral.” That fascination drives Luk’s debut feature, which world premieres in competition at the Edinburgh International Film Festival. Starring Olivia Luccardi , James Cusati-Moyer and Romina D’Ugo, the Canada-Italy production follows three estranged siblings reuniting in rural Italy after middle sister Miriam (Olivia Luccardi) is released from psychiatric treatment following an experience she understands as a spiritual awakening rather than a breakdown. She knows herself and she makes choices. However, when she becomes a figure that people rally around, people are imbuing her with meaning. When she becomes abstract, she no longer controls the message.” Popular on Variety That uncertainty extends to the film itself, which slips between psychological drama, comedy and magical realism without settling comfortably into any of them. For Luk, the tonal slipperiness developed naturally from writing. “I set up the situation and these characters, and as I’m writing, I’m following what they’re doing. What I’m waiting for is how they surprise me,” she says. Courtesy of Nicolás Villegas One influence was Marco Ferreri’s “La Grande Bouffe,” the grotesque story of four men attempting to eat themselves to death. “The comedy is following through that premise in a serious way, because if you actually are going to eat yourself to death, you’re going to have gastrointestinal problems,” Luk says. “It’s also very silly. It never takes itself too seriously.” Italian cinema was integral to “Sacred Creatures” from the start. Luk points to films of the 1970s, admiring their willingness to move between modes contemporary cinema can sometimes keep separate. “A lot of the ’70s movies, especially European ones, are completely in between genres.” Luccardi was similarly keen to avoid reducing Miriam to a diagnosis. “She is healing from the lack of belief from people and everyone thinking that something was wrong with her,” Luccardi explains, adding that Miriam feels “meant for something greater.” There was another, less metaphysical piece of direction that unlocked the character: Luk told her Miriam was like a cat. “She’s very much like: ‘I’m letting you in on my terms. No, I actually don’t want you to touch me. I want to be a pet, but not like that,’” laughs Luccardi. “I did a lot of cat direction,” Luk dryly admits. As Miriam grows more secure in herself, Luccardi subtly changed the physical quality of the performance. “There was more of a calmness in my breath,” she says. “She was more relaxed and calm and just flowed. Before, she may have been a little more stressed and tightly wound.” That growing self-possession becomes visual in the film’s party scene, where Miriam arrives in a voluminous yellow-green dress that immediately separates her from the room around her. There is something of Bette Davis’ party entrance in “All About Eve” to the moment: costume becomes a declaration of presence, allowing Miriam to suddenly occupy a different plane from everyone watching her. Luk wanted the dress to be “kind of ridiculous looking, but also kind of chic,” something that would “take up some space” without seeming entirely out of place. “Miriam is new and a little ridiculous,” she says, with its uncontained “fluffiness” signalling “an irreverence to what has come before.” Luccardi’s relationship with it was rather less reverential by the end of the shoot. “At the beginning, it was great. At the end… I wore it a long time,” she jokes. “As with every costume, you love it at the beginning and then you’re like: ‘Can we burn it, please?’” Courtesy of Nicolás Villegas The surrounding family remain skeptical of their sister’s burgeoning allure to those around her. Luk, an only child who grew up surrounded by cousins, was amused by the way relatives can inhabit incompatible versions of the same history. “They’re always competing,” she says. The instinct of creating a story that makes life easier to comprehend ultimately expands beyond the siblings. Luk grew up without religion, but many childhood friends were religious and invited her to churches and youth groups. Watching from the outside, she was intrigued by their ability to surrender themselves to faith. “I would watch them read a text and believe in that text and treat it like this holy thing,” she recalls. “It was really hard for me to give myself over to something like that.” At Catholic services, she found herself captivated by the incense, clothing and ceremony. “I was like: ‘This is so fun and theatrical.’ I can see how it could be really comforting,” she says. “There’s a community-oriented spirit to it. Being a fan of a big sport is kind of fun. Yelling at a team is fun.” The director began thinking about fandoms, sports and social media with much the same curiosity. What separates a few people who regularly gather from a movement? “What if people hung out, and then that becomes a movement?” she says. “A few people hang out, and then more people hang out. Then you do it regularly, and what happens?” The film is shot in Piedmont and Italy provided a fertile landscape for those questions. Luk recalls seeing reports about a teenage protester and wondering why there couldn’t be a patron saint for protest, and what the origin story of a new saint might look like. But after all that construction of a film, a family history, a faith and perhaps even a saint, the director isn’t interested in providing audiences with a final answer about Miriam. “I want people to come away examining why they believe in something and how,” she says, “and that there is a pleasure in believing something.” “You never know if you are right or you are wrong. You might be wrong.” Or, as Luccardi puts it: “You never know if someone’s crazy or if someone’s enlightened. Who knows?” “It’s a fine line.” Prime Video’s Docuseries ‘Murder 101’ Moves Beyond Crime to Showcase the Power of Community: TV Review Prime Video’s Stunning Drama ’Sterling Point’ Elevates the YA Genre Beyond the Mundane: TV Review Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham Are Badass Besties in Prime Video’s Middling Action Dramedy ‘Ride or Die’: TV Review Loading comments... title: ‘Lanterns’ Bosses and Stars on How the Show’s Grounded Approach Ushers in an ‘Entirely Different Kind of Superhero’
full_text: Aug 15, 2026 1:30pm PT ‘Lanterns’ Bosses and Stars on How the Show’s Grounded Approach Ushers in an ‘Entirely Different Kind of Superhero’ By Matt Minton Plus Icon Matt Minton mminton@variety.com Latest ‘The Pitt,’ ‘Hacks’ and ‘Beef’ Among Astra TV Awards Winners 4 hours ago Slipknot Confirms Sid Wilson’s Sudden Exit: ‘We Wish Him the Best’ 12 hours ago ‘Lanterns’ Bosses and Stars on How the Show’s Grounded Approach Ushers in an ‘Entirely Different Kind of Superhero’ 13 hours ago See All Courtesy of Warner Bros. Discovery As part of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s newly expanded DCU, a more grounded take on the “Green Lantern” comics may surprise audiences who associate the character with the Ryan Reynolds film that received poor reviews back in 2011. But for co-creators Chris Mundy , Damon Lindelof and Tom King , “ Lanterns ” is all about going back to the original iteration of the character when he was “an entirely different kind of superhero.” Related Stories Mubi to Release ‘La Mesías,’ From ‘La Bola Negra’ Cannes Best Director Winners, in the U.K., Germany, Canada, Australia and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE) “We’re talking about almost a century’s worth of storytelling, and now we get to carry that baton,” Lindelof told Variety . “But then at the same time, the audience is hungry for something original and relevant, and they want storytellers to take risks. Those risks can’t feel like they’re gimmicks; they have to feel like they have real emotional stakes.” Popular on Variety The show follows Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) as he is forced to take John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) under his wing as a backup. As the Green Lantern, Hal has the power to create material items through his ring and acts as an intergalactic space officer. Things take a dark turn after a series of unexplainable deaths draw Hal and John to a small town in Nebraska. As creators, King brings a wealth of experience as a comic book writer, while Lindelof created the “Watchmen” TV series. Mundy, who served as showrunner on “Ozark,” is new to the comic book world. “I know that if Damon didn’t work on this show, I would have used — and I think Tom would say the same — ‘Watchmen’ as a real touchstone of how you do a show and have it be emotional and about real people, while also honoring the comic book part of it,” Mundy said. In addition to the grounded approach that “Watchmen” takes, “Lanterns” also shares similarities in how the show explores race, colonization and justice. King explained how “there’s a wonderful coincidental parallel with comics that ‘Watchmen,’ in the ’80s, set the standard for a generation of comic book writers who were like, ‘Oh, we can talk about those themes using superheroes!'” Poorna Jagannathan, who plays the conniving and mysterious Zoe, hopes that shows like “Lanterns” invite more actors into the DCU who don’t read comic books. “I thought I’d be with a green screen wearing a suit, talking to no one at all, just into the abyss,” she told Variety at Thursday’s premiere on the Paramount lot. “I hesitated because I didn’t know this world at all. I felt like I didn’t belong, actually. I felt bad that I was so ignorant about it.” “I don’t think that only this universe will be affected by it; I think every show in the genre will be affected by what happened on ‘Lanterns,'” she added. “It’ll be a blueprint on how to take something big and keep it with a beating heart.” As the DCU continues to expand and test the waters of audiences, both with the success of films like “Superman” and the underwhelming reception to “Supergirl,” how audiences react to “Lanterns” could determine if early conversations about Season 2 turn into an official renewal. “The one thing that fans hate more than being listened to is fan service and that sort of idea of doing something just to placate them. And so I do think that fandom is not a monolith,” Lindelof said of navigating fandom expectations. “There are some fans who want more risky, edgy sort of revisionist storytelling inside of these adaptations, and some fans who are just basically like, ‘Give me what I love.'” There are certain canonical elements that the “Lanterns” team had to carefully maneuver, such as how the show ties into John Stewart’s involvement in “Man of Tomorrow,” and the return of Guy Gardner (Nathan Fillion), who also appears in “Superman” and “Peacemaker.” But when it comes to what “Lanterns” might signal for the future of the newly revamped DCU, it’s all about creative voices being at the forefront. “You can’t go out of bounds in terms of storylines that James and Peter want to do,” Lindelof said. “But artistically, they’re giving us a lot of freedom to tell the story how we want.” “Lanterns” premieres Sunday, Aug. 16 on HBO Max. title: ‘The Beast in Me’ Showrunner Knows That the Violent Murder Scene Was a “Potential Tune-Out Point” For Some Viewers
full_text: × Skip to main content By Beatrice Verhoeven Plus Icon Beatrice Verhoeven Awards Editor bverhoeven Follow Sign Up View All August 15, 2026 1:00pm Matthew Rhys as Nile Jarvis Chris Saunders/Netflix The Beast in Me showrunner Howard Gordon knows there was one scene in the Netflix limited series that was divisive because of its brutality. “There were people for whom that was a potential tune-out point. Maybe some others tuned in extra because of it. It’s hard to tell,” Gordon, producer of 24 and Homeland , tells THR . The scene in question is — spoiler alert — the flashback scene in which Nile Jarvis’ (Matthew Rhys) wife, Madison (Leila George), is violently killed. The moment answers the question the entire show sets up, and the question Claire Danes’ character, Aggie, who is grappling with the death of her son, tries to answer while writing a book about her mysterious neighbor: Did he or didn’t he kill his wife? Related Stories TV The TikTok Comment That Let Megan Gallagher Know She Nailed the Representation of Motherhood in 'All Her Fault' TV 'Paradise' Executive Producer Explains Why Julianne Nicholson's Character Had to Go Down with the Bunker in Season 2 Gordon breaks down with THR why The Beast in Me was a hard premise to tackle and why Rhys was the right guy to play Nile. I know Gabe Rotter wrote this six or seven years ago, and it took a while to gain momentum. Why do you think it was such a difficult premise to get moving? A couple things. I think the secret of the pilot and Gabe’s creation is a character who is a writer [Danes], who is stuck really in this existential kind of “stuckness” because of this terrible loss. Those things were very evident in the premise. But when she has a killer move in next door, or someone she suspects to be that, and writes this book … writing a book about somebody is a pretty static idea, so we had to find the dramatics of what happens. What does that cat-and-mouse actually look like? Nile in the earlier version was kind of exiled to the suburbs but was painting. These two solitary characters who don’t have a lot of people around them, that’s not a very dramatic premise. It’s a very challenging premise. So we gave Nile [the real estate development] Jarvis Yards. He has still been exiled, but he still has a very important hand in a very big, controversial development. And who is his father? And Aggie’s relationship had to be explored. There were a lot of balls in the air, but what was evident to us was this essential loss, this essential grief, which is the most unimaginable thing any of us can go through and that universal fact of loss and how it can bend us. But there were too many multiple traumas and trauma swappings that wound up obscuring the issues. So most of it was about clearing the brush and finding the story. Before the final reveal, the audience is constantly left wondering whether Nile did it or didn’t. How did you keep it in the gray zone? The journey of whether he is or isn’t [a killer] … keeping that possibility open [was important], but ultimately we have to also look at the audience’s awareness of: If he wasn’t, where would the story go? We planted certain flags at various points. Part of the other problem was that there were these backstories of Aggie’s own loss, of Nile’s previous marriage and that unsolved mystery. So there’s a lot of backstory, which, you don’t want to be reading headlines for an entire eight episodes. So you have to bring the backstory into the present and keep it alive. When you ask what the storytelling challenge was, the idea of a guy who you meet, and at the end of the pilot, you’ve now whispered your darkest secret to him [that Aggie wished her son’s killer was dead], and then that darkest secret becomes enacted makes very little sense. I mean, what was he hoping to achieve here by doing that? Only when refracted through the prism of a sociopath can you answer that question. So when you’re looking for rational cause and effect within the parameters of a healthy human being with a conscience, you’re not going to find very many answers there. You have to embrace the sociopathy in that way. As for how we did it: As a showrunner, you really take the temperature of the people who are readers and your fellow writers and your actors. How do you keep people leaning forward and wanting to watch the next episode? What did you see in Matthew for this incredibly complex, terrifying role? We had high expectations, but he blew them away. I will say that the character of Nile Jarvis was the hardest to figure out and decode. The language of a sociopath is very easy to have a mustached, twirly guy speaking and pontificating and vaguely threatening tropes, but to really give him a kind of humanity, vulnerability. … I think Matthew’s secret was not just to make him charming, but to make him, by turns, dangerous and vulnerable. So he took the music that we gave him and just made it better. He’s a charming guy, so you bring that kind of charm to bear on a character as ruthless and damaged as Nile. And look, this is an improbable love affair. What was also interesting was to have a love affair and to take sex out of the equation really made it great, made it so much fun, and these are two people who are uncomfortably alike who find each other and actually connect in a way. But then with that love comes the inevitable betrayal that he feels once Aggie, his new friend, turns out to be after him. The eventual murder scene is very violent. Where do you draw the line in how graphic you want to go with scenes like this? I tended to be the grandpa in the production. I have to bring [executive producer] Antonio Campos into this equation. Antonio obviously was the captain of the ship on the set, but he really was an active producer as well, so there is a sort of rough democracy. Being the showrunner, I got to cast the winning vote often, but I do hear it when I’m outvoted. In instances like that, where I felt it was, “Whoa,” where I was a little squeamish, you have to just embrace that this is a really violent moment, and this is a very broken, evil, awful person. And you may as well go all in — in for a dime, in for a dollar. A lot of it is seasoned to taste, and I think there were people for whom that was a potential tune-out point. Maybe some people tuned in extra because of it. It’s hard to tell. At the end of the day, you have to be the sort of lightning-rod litmus test for your audience. That really felt like it was consistent with the tone and the texture. This story first appeared in an August stand-alone issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. To receive the magazine,

title: The TikTok Comment That Let Megan Gallagher Know She Nailed the Representation of Motherhood in ‘All Her Fault’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Brande Victorian Plus Icon Brande Victorian Deputy Awards Editor View All August 15, 2026 12:30pm Sarah Snook and Jake Lacy in All Her Fault Sarah Enticknap/PEACOCK Megan Gallagher is something of an adaptation whisperer. The writer and executive producer whose credits include the BBC miniseries Wolf , based on the Jack Caffery novels by Mo Hayder, and the upcoming ITV drama The Blame , adapted from Charlotte Langley’s novel, delivered Peacock’s most watched original series to date — 46 million hours viewed in its first three weeks — with All Her Fault . The adaptation of Andrea Mara’s best-selling novel stars Sarah Snook as Marissa, a mother in distress when her son, Milo (Duke McCloud), goes missing and secrets about everyone in her inner circle — particularly her husband, Peter (Jake Lacy) — begin to unfold, raising doubt about their culpability. But more than a thriller, the Emmy-nominated limited series created a dialogue about parenthood — specifically the unspoken feeling of being a single mother, even in a partnered relationship — which Gallagher was all too eager to explore. Related Stories TV 'Paradise' Executive Producer Explains Why Julianne Nicholson's Character Had to Go Down with the Bunker in Season 2 TV 'Heated Rivalry,' 'Hacks' Top GALECA Dorian TV Awards Winners List Sarah Snook initially said there was no way she could do this series, and then you told her you could shoot in Australia and she said yes. What was it about her and this role that wouldn’t let you take no for an answer? For the majority of the series, Marissa is in DEFCON 5 trauma. A mother’s worst nightmare: child missing, at any moment you could get the call that he’s dead; it doesn’t get any worse than that. Because of that, we knew that there was going to be a lot of crying. And you need such an incredible actress for a role like that because if you don’t, you can lose a character in the crying. The crying can become the dominant thing, and the acting is the crying as opposed to being able to convey a personality underneath all of that, being able to find the nuance of who this character is outside of the crying. The way that we cry, the way that we emote, the way that we break down, it’s not universal. So I wanted an actress who could handle all that, not just somebody who would be a good crier but somebody who’s really sophisticated, and she so thoroughly and ridiculously fit that bill. How did you pull off moving the setting of the book from Dublin to Chicago and shooting in Australia? So I’m American, but I live in Norway. My producers are in London. The broadcaster’s in L.A. We shot it in Melbourne, and it’s set in Chicago, where I’ve never been. So it’s a testament to how everybody’s global. Andrea’s books — and I’m working on another [adaptation] of hers now — on one end, they’re really interesting because who doesn’t like looking at Ireland, but the stories themselves are, for the most part, quite universal and can translate anywhere. So there was nothing culturally about the story that she told that couldn’t easily be translated to America. In terms of setting it in Chicago, once we knew we were doing it in America, what mattered to us is that the show felt accessible and relatable to all Americans. That’s why we didn’t want New York or L.A. or Miami. Those cities have such distinct personalities, whereas Chicago was very Middle America and more universally understandable. How did we pull it off though? A hell of a lot of postproduction. In the book, the investigator on Milo’s case is a woman. How did Michael Peña end up as Detective Alcaras in the series? The detective is a very small character in the book named McConville. So that character — Andrea wouldn’t mind me saying this — that’s entirely me. It felt like in a show that was quite critical, obviously, of men, that having some positive male energy in there was not just the right thing to do in terms of ticking boxes, but the fair thing to do. I have a son who’s quite disabled, and my husband’s an incredible father and really runs the show. I wanted to touch upon that from a very personal place. And it just felt like in a show that’s so critical of men and of men not being involved on the home front, why not show a man who is — despite the fact that he’s got one of the more complicated home fronts you could possibly have. Alcaras still takes his son to school. He still knows the names of the other kids. He still knows the teachers. He still packs his son’s lunch. He still does pickups. That all came from my heart and soul. The big conversation that was had on social media about the series was the representation of the realities of parenting, particularly motherhood. Is there any aspect of that response that surprised you? I knew that the theme would resonate with women. I’m the neurotic, worried writer. I think, “Oh, it’s going to be terrible, it’s never going to come together, it’s not going to work.” That’s me. But I was quietly confident about that theme because every woman I know in my age bracket who is working and raising kids is just breaking down in their car crying, and they don’t understand how it’s supposed to all get done. And we’ve seen little bits and pieces of it on TV, but we haven’t really seen it front and center. I knew this isn’t just me and my friends. This is everyone. So why the fuck isn’t it on television? So I knew it would resonate. I did not know it would resonate as much as it did. I don’t know if I could say I’m surprised. I’m just really pleased. And every little, tiny breadcrumb-y feminist thing that I put in there — even the most subtle stuff — is all over TikTok. It was dissected endlessly. The nicest response that I saw was a comment on TikTok that said, “These are two of the worst husbands I’ve ever seen on television and neither one of them was having an affair.” We’ve seen affairs a hundred million times, and that’s not always the most hurtful thing you could do. The series’ ending is satisfying on so many levels, but I’m curious, were there any alternate endings you considered that were particularly intriguing? No. The way that it plays out in the series is unique to the series. The sequence of events, like [Milo’s abductor Carrie, played by Sophia Lillis] being at the house — Carrie never shows up at the house in the book or any of that kind of stuff. However, the broad strokes of Peter switching the babies early on, which is why Carrie did what she did, and Marissa killing Peter is 100 percent in the book. And I completely give credit to Andrea Mara. So many thrillers start out great and then the ending is just kind of [blah], whereas this was a whopper of an ending. So no one considered anything else ever, because you don’t mess with something [that good]. It’s like the opening. The opening of the series is the opening of the book. And no one ever considered anything else because there is no better way to open. There is no better way to close. You also have Such a Nice Girl coming, which is another adaptation from Andrea Mara. Anything you can foreshadow about this new project? Such a Nice Girl is a really fun read and it’s a great examination of female friendship that crosses two generations. There are two characters who are late 40s, early 50s. And the story is about a crime that appears to have taken place between their two daughters who are also best friends. It’s twisty-turny. It takes place over just a day, so it’s really, really tight. But just like with her other stories, there’s something to say about female friendship and the power of it that’s just really, really satisfying. We’re diving into it right now and it’s really fun. title: Hollywood Flashback: When Dudley Moore Intoxicated Audiences in ‘Arthur’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All August 15, 2026 12:00pm Dudley Moore became best known for the title role in 'Arthur,' which landed Oscars for supporting actor John Gielgud and for the original song “Arthur’s Theme (Best That You Can Do).” Warner Brothers/courtesy Everett Collection A toast is in order for Arthur , which became a comedy classic despite a quiet release 45 years ago. After penning Carl Reiner’s 1978 comedy The One and Only starring Henry Winkler, Steve Gordon was hired to direct his own Arthur script for Orion . Gordon initially considered George Segal and John Belushi for the title role before casting Dudley Moore off the success of 10 , in which the actor starred opposite Bo Derek. Arthur centers on alcoholic playboy Arthur Bach, who will be cut off from his family fortune unless he marries a woman he doesn’t love, which becomes complicated when he falls for working-class Linda, played by Liza Minnelli . At the time, Moore praised the script for its barrage of jokes: “Ten laughs a page, instead of one laugh every 10 pages.” Related Stories Hollywood Flashback Helloooo, Emmy: Art Carney's Enduring 'Honeymooners' Triumph Hollywood Flashback 40 Years Ago, Rob Reiner Turned Stephen King's Most Personal Story Into a Surprise Hit Actress Anne DeSalvo, who played sex worker Gloria, tells The Hollywood Reporter that Moore, a classically trained pianist, would warmly greet her on set. “Dudley would be playing the piano, and he’d say, ‘Good morning, Anne,’ ” she recalls. “He was such a gentleman.” The lead character was written as American, but Moore convinced Gordon to let him keep his British accent: “Steve kept phoning me up and saying, ‘Are you sure you can’t do an American accent?’ I told him if I tried, it would be the most distorted performance.” Arthur hit theaters on July 17, 1981, with THR ‘s review extolling the “hilarious comedy” and Moore’s “impeccable timing.” The film got off to a slow box office start amid marketing challenges, but word of mouth drew crowds for weeks to come, as Arthur became the year’s fourth-highest-grossing title. The film earned four Oscar nominations, winning for best supporting actor for John Gielgud as butler Hobson. It also won an Academy Award for Christopher Cross’ main theme song, “Best That You Can Do” — co-written by Burt Bacharach and Carole Bayer Sager — which hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Gordon died suddenly of a heart attack a year later at age 44, making Arthur his only feature. Moore and Minnelli returned for a 1988 sequel, while a 2011 remake starred Russell Brand , Jennifer Garner, Greta Gerwig and Helen Mirren, but neither matched the success of the original, which was named one of AFI’s top 100 comedies. Moore, who died in 2002 at age 66 after battling progressive supranuclear palsy, once called Arthur his favorite role: “I love the character.” This story appeared in the Aug. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.
